criteria_quotes: “Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (CPT 23472)” and “Total shoulder arthroplasty (CPT 23472)” may be medically necessary “when all the following criteria are met.”
“A. There is no active infection in the shoulder joint; and”

“B. At least two of the following are met: 1. Pain interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs); or 2. Pain is increased with initiation of activity; or 3. Pain occurs with range of motion (ROM)”

“C. Imaging confirms any of the following” conditions: “intra-articular fracture” meeting the stated requirements; “nonunion or malunion of an articular fracture”; “irreparable or massive rotator cuff tear”; “bone tumor involving the shoulder”; “avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis)” with humeral-head collapse plus limited range of motion or crepitus; or osteoarthritis/post-traumatic arthritis meeting the policy’s additional requirements.

For osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis, the policy requires “either limited range of motion or crepitus with glenohumeral joint rotation” and either “imaging shows bone-on-bone contact” or continued symptoms despite conservative treatment within the last year plus at least two listed structural findings, such as subchondral cysts, subchondral sclerosis, periarticular osteophytes, joint subluxation, joint-space narrowing, bony glenoid deformity, or other structural pathology.
The policy states: “Initial shoulder joint replacement is considered not medically necessary when criteria I. or II. above are not met.”

The documentation requirements include: “Indication for the requested surgery”; clinical documentation of “extent and response to conservative care”; documentation of “the extent and specifics of one or more of the functional impairments or disabilities”; imaging completed “within the past 12 months,” with documented interpretation; and any “criteria-specific lab values or reports.”

The policy defines conservative treatment within the last year as at least three weeks of an NSAID, acetaminophen, or corticosteroid injection; at least six weeks of physical therapy, occupational therapy, or home exercise; and activity modification for at least six weeks. An exception to physical therapy may be permitted when clearly documented.

There is no active infection in the shoulder joint; and B. At least two of the following are met (1.-3.) 1. Pain interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs); or 2. Pain is increased with initiation of activity; or 3. Pain occurs with range of motion (ROM); and C. Imaging confirms any of the following (1.-6.): 1. Intra-articular fracture showing humeral head fracture in at least 3 parts with repair not achievable by open reduction and fixation; or 2. Nonunion or malunion of an articular fracture; or 3. Irreparable or massive rotator cuff tear; or 4. Bone tumor involving the shoulder; or 5. Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) and patient has humeral head collapse with either limited range of motion or crepitus with glenohumeral joint rotation; or 6. Osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis and the following criteria are met (a.-b.): a. Member has either limited range of motion or crepitus with glenohumeral joint rotation; and b. Either of the following are met: i. Imaging shows bone-on-bone contact; or ii. Member has continued symptoms despite conservative treatments within the last year and at least two of the following are present (i.- vii.): a. Subchondral cysts; or b. Subchondral sclerosis; or c. Periarticular osteophytes; or d. Joint subluxation; or e. Joint space narrowing; or f. Bony glenoid deformity; or g. Other structural pathology; II. Initial shoulder joint replacement may be considered medically necessary for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis when all the following criteria (A.-E.) are met: A. There is no active infection of the shoulder joint; and B. At least two of the following criteria are met (1.-4.): 1. Pain interferes with activities of daily living (ADLs); or 2. Pain is increased with initiation of activity; or 3. Pain occurs with range of motion (ROM); or Page 4 of 13 MP430 4. Pain at night; and C. Either of the following are met (1.-2.) 1. Limited range of motion; or 2. Crepitus with glenohumeral joint rotation; and D. Imaging documents at least two of the following (1.-6.): 1. Subchondral cysts; or 2. Marginal erosions; or 3. Periarticular osteopenia; or 4. Joint space narrowing; or 5. Joint subluxation; or 6. Bony glenoid deformity; and E. The patient has failed conservative treatment within the past year, including all of the following (1.-3.): 1. Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for at least 12 weeks; and 2. At least 12 weeks of physical therapy, occupational therapy, or home exercise unless contraindicated (See Policy Guidelines); and 3. Activity modification for at least 12 weeks. III. Initial shoulder joint replacement is considered not medically necessary when criteria I. or II. above are not met. Shoulder Joint Removal, Replacement, Revision IV. Shoulder arthroplasty removal, replacement or revision may be considered medically necessary with joint infection when imaging confirms any of the following criteria (A.-F.): A. Imaging documents sinus tract is communicating with prosthetic joint B. Prosthetic joint infection by positive synovial fluid culture or tissue culture and one of the following conditions is present: 1. Two cultures are positive for same organism or 2. Culture positive for Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) or 3. Culture positive for gram negative organism or 4. Culture positive for Enterococci; or C. Joint pain present or erythema or drainage or swelling at joint by physical examination and 2 of the following criteria are met: 1. Temperature > 100.4 °F (38.0 °C) 2. Synovial WBC or neutrophil percentage > normal 3. ESR > 30 mm/hr 4. CRP > normal 5. Elevated synovial alpha-defensin D. Joint pain is present with high suspicion of infection, and either of the following conditions is present: 1. Loosening of the implant; or 2. Ongoing shoulder stiffness with no known cause outside of infection; V. Shoulder arthroplasty removal, replacement or revision may be considered medically necessary with no active joint infection when imaging confirms any of the following criteria Page 5 of 13 MP430 (A.-G.): A. Failed rotator cuff tendon after index arthroplasty by imaging B. Malpositioned or ill-fitting prosthesis component C. Periprosthetic fracture D. Prosthesis breakage E. Recurrent dislocation or instability F. Symptomatic aseptic loosening of prosthesis or cement G. Worn or dislocated plastic insert VI. Shoulder arthroplasty removal, replacement or revision is considered not medically necessary when criteria IV and V above are not met. Page 6 of 13 MP430 DEFINITIONS Activities of Daily Living The activities of daily living (ADLs) is a term used to describe essential skills that are required to independently care for oneself. Examples may include, but are not limited to, the following: • Ambulating • Feeding • Dressing • Personal hygiene • Transportation and shopping • Meal preparation • Housecleaning and home maintenance Conservative treatment Conservative treatment within the last year includes all of the following: 1. At least 3 weeks of NSAIDs or acetaminophen or a corticosteroid injection; and 1. At least 6 weeks of physical therapy, occupational therapy, or home exercise; and 2. Activity modification for at least 6 weeks. Exception to physical therapy requirement may be permitted (e.g., intractable pain so severe that physical therapy is contraindicated) when clearly documented in medical records. BACKGROUND Reverse shoulder arthroplasty Reverse shoulder arthroplasty is a surgical procedure where the normal ball-and-socket structure of the shoulder is reversed. The ball component is attached to the shoulder blade, and the socket is attached to the top of the arm bone. This technique is used to improve function and reduce pain in patients with rotator cuff tears, arthritis, severe bone deformity, or previous failed shoulder surgeries. Shoulder hemiarthroplasty Shoulder hemiarthroplasty is a surgical procedure where only the head of the humerus (the ball) is replaced with a prosthetic implant, while the socket (glenoid) is left intact. This is often performed in cases where the humeral head is severely damaged, but the glenoid is still healthy. It helps in relieving pain and restoring shoulder function. Enrollee claim submissions A claim is a request to an insurance company for payment of health care services. Usually, Providers file claims with us on your behalf. Payments for most Services are made directly to Providers. Member claims submissions To file a claim, follow these steps: Complete a claim form . Attach a copy of receipt, provider invoice that includes the provider tax ID number, CPT codes, dates of service, ICD-10 codes (diagnosis codes), billed and paid amount with your proof of payment. Time frames for processing claims Clean claims will be processed within 30 days of receipt of your Claim. We will send an Explanation of Benefits (or EOB, see below) to you that will explain how your Claim was processed. If Providence denies your claim, the EOB will contain an explanation of the denial. If we need additional time to process your Claim, we will explain the reason in a notice of delay that we will send you within 30 days after receiving your Claim.     "The policy defines conservative treatment within the last year as at least three weeks of an NSAID, acetaminophen, or corticosteroid injection; at least six weeks of physical therapy, occupational therapy, or home exercise; and activity modification for at least six weeks.
